lesson_title: How a Marula Seed Hitches a Ride
hook_text: A marula seed's best travel plan? Get eaten by an elephant.
clip_script: It starts with pollen landing on a marula flower's sticky stigma. The pollen grain grows a tunnel, a pollen tube, down to an ovule, and a male cell joins the egg cell. That is fertilisation. Now the petals fall off. The ovule becomes a seed with a baby plant inside. The ovary swells into a juicy fruit. Here is the clever part. A seed that drops under its parent is crowded out. So the marula makes a fruit elephants love. The elephant eats it, walks for kilometres, and drops the seed in a pile of dung, a free trip plus fertiliser. Other plants have other tickets: blackjacks hook onto your socks, dandelions fly on parachutes, coconuts float across oceans, and bean pods simply pop and fling their seeds.
visual_style: Whiteboard pollen tube racing down a style; a flower morphing into a marula fruit; a cartoon elephant walking a dotted path and leaving a seed that sprouts; quick icons of hooks, parachutes, a coconut and a popping pod.
pacing: Quick fertilisation sequence, a comic elephant trip, rapid-fire dispersal montage.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and work out how every seed in your garden travels.
